forces: Orchestra, arranged by Gordon Jacob from the military-band original
intro: A march, an intermezzo and a second march built from nine English folk songs, written for a military band and played here in an orchestral arrangement. The Columbia Broadcasting Symphony under Howard Barlow recorded it in December 1939.

sections.label: III · March, Folk Songs from Somerset

cues.title: Seventeen Come Sunday
cues.text: The first march opens with the folk song Seventeen Come Sunday, heard first from woodwinds and strings. Its irregular phrasing gives the march a syncopated, quirky swing.
cues.evidence: Alex Burns, Classicalexburns (21 November 2022), on the orchestral version: the song is “first heard by the woodwinds and strings” and its irregular phrasing gives a syncopated quirkiness. https://classicalexburns.com/2022/11/21/ralph-vaughan-williams-english-folk-song-suite-memorable-melodies/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Pretty Caroline, solo clarinet
cues.text: A gentler second song, Pretty Caroline, is led by a solo clarinet after a short two-bar bridge that changes the key.
cues.evidence: Burgess Hill Symphony Orchestra programme note (Barry Fogden): a two-bar bridge changes the key and connects the first tune to “the gentle Pretty Caroline”; Burns: the tune is “led by a solo clarinet”. https://www.bhso.org.uk/work/vaughan-williams-english-folk-song-suite-4/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dives and Lazarus in 6/8
cues.text: Dives and Lazarus enters in the lower instruments in 6/8, while the upper winds flutter in a straight 2/4 above it. The two rhythms rub against each other until the reprise.
cues.evidence: Burns: Vaughan Williams writes the Dives and Lazarus countermelody in 6/8 rhythms “with the upper orchestra playing straight 2/4 rhythms”; the reprise relieves the unease. https://classicalexburns.com/2022/11/21/ralph-vaughan-williams-english-folk-song-suite-memorable-melodies/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Written for Kneller Hall
cues.text: Vaughan Williams wrote the suite in 1923 for the Royal Military School of Music at Kneller Hall, where it was first played on 4 July 1923. Gordon Jacob made the orchestral transcription the following year.
cues.evidence: Burgess Hill Symphony Orchestra programme note: written at the request of the Royal Military School of Music at Kneller Hall, transcribed for orchestra the following year by Gordon Jacob; Alex Burns, Classicalexburns: premièred on 4 July 1923 at Kneller Hall. https://www.bhso.org.uk/work/vaughan-williams-english-folk-song-suite-4/

cues.title: The march comes round again
cues.text: The reprise brings the opening material back. The movement ends on a Picardy third, a major chord closing music that has leaned toward the minor.
cues.evidence: Burns: the unease is “soon relieved as the reprise begins”; Burgess Hill Symphony Orchestra programme note: “the very last chord … is what is called a Picardy Third”. https://www.bhso.org.uk/work/vaughan-williams-english-folk-song-suite-4/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A chill chord, then the oboe
cues.text: A chilling minor chord introduces the slow Intermezzo. A solo oboe sings My Bonny Boy in the F Dorian mode, and the lower instruments repeat it.
cues.evidence: Burgess Hill Symphony Orchestra programme note: “A chilling minor chord introduces the slow Intermezzo”; Burns: the movement is opened by a solo oboe, “in the F dorian mode”, repeated by the lower orchestra. https://classicalexburns.com/2022/11/21/ralph-vaughan-williams-english-folk-song-suite-memorable-melodies/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Songs from the road
cues.text: In the few years after 1903 Vaughan Williams spent every free moment out on the road collecting songs from their elderly singers, most of which had never been written down. He covered much of the country by bicycle and train and amassed over 800.
cues.evidence: Barry Fogden’s programme note for the Burgess Hill Symphony Orchestra: in the few years after 1903 Vaughan Williams spent every free moment out on the road collecting songs, covering more or less the whole country by bicycle and train and amassing over 800. https://www.bhso.org.uk/work/vaughan-williams-english-folk-song-suite-4/

cues.title: Green Bushes, poco allegro
cues.text: Midway through the Intermezzo a solo violin leads into a Poco allegro on Green Bushes, a waltz-like tune that relieves the tension of the opening.
cues.evidence: Burns: a solo violin “leads the music into the Poco allegro section”, based on Green Bushes, “this waltz section”. https://classicalexburns.com/2022/11/21/ralph-vaughan-williams-english-folk-song-suite-memorable-melodies/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: My Bonny Boy in fragments
cues.text: The first melody comes back in a much more fragmented form, and the mysterious atmosphere settles once more. The movement dies away to a quiet close on an even more striking Picardy third.
cues.evidence: Burns: the first melody is “played once more … in a much more fragmented manner” and the music is “drawn to a quiet close”; Burgess Hill Symphony Orchestra programme note: “an even more striking Picardy Third to finish”. https://classicalexburns.com/2022/11/21/ralph-vaughan-williams-english-folk-song-suite-memorable-melodies/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Blow Away the Morning Dew
cues.text: The final march opens with a catchy introduction, and the clarinet takes the solo line on Blow Away the Morning Dew. The melody is passed around the orchestra.
cues.evidence: Burns: the movement opens with “a catchy introduction” and the clarinet “takes the solo line”; the melody is “passed around the orchestra”. https://classicalexburns.com/2022/11/21/ralph-vaughan-williams-english-folk-song-suite-memorable-melodies/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: High Germany, trumpets on top
cues.text: The second tune, High Germany, is led by the lower instruments, with the trumpets adding a sparkling fanfare above.
cues.evidence: Burns: “The second melody, based on High Germany, is led by the lower instruments, with the trumpets adding a sparkling fanfare on top.” https://classicalexburns.com/2022/11/21/ralph-vaughan-williams-english-folk-song-suite-memorable-melodies/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: John Barleycorn, the heavy one
cues.text: The last tune, John Barleycorn, is the heaviest of the four. Trombones and basses lead, and a decorative melody plays above them.
cues.evidence: Burns: the final melody “is based on John Barleycorn, and is the heaviest of all the melodies in this movement”, led by trombones and basses with a decorative melody above. https://classicalexburns.com/2022/11/21/ralph-vaughan-williams-english-folk-song-suite-memorable-melodies/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Columbia, December 1939
cues.text: The Columbia Broadcasting Symphony under Howard Barlow recorded the suite on 19 December 1939, with an oboe solo in the Intermezzo played by Mitch Miller. It appeared in March 1940 as Columbia Masterworks set X-159.
cues.evidence: The Internet Archive item’s description of the Columbia set X-159 (recorded 19 December 1939; side list; oboe solo credited to Mitch Miller); Discogs release 13526665 for the English Columbia issue, DB 1930–1931. https://archive.org/details/x-159-rvw-english-folksong-suite

cues.title: A reprise and a big chord
cues.text: A reprise of the opening tune ends the march abruptly and good-humouredly. The whole orchestra strikes a final big chord.
cues.evidence: Burgess Hill Symphony Orchestra programme note: a repeat of the first tune “brings proceedings to an abrupt and good-humoured end”; Burns: the movement ends with a reprise “before a final big chord is played from the whole orchestra”. https://www.bhso.org.uk/work/vaughan-williams-english-folk-song-suite-4/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Columbia Broadcasting Symphony (orchestra), Howard Barlow (conductor), Mitch Miller (oboe solo in the Intermezzo)
fields.note: The orchestra and conductor are credited by both sources. The oboe soloist is named only in the Archive item’s side list.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral arrangement by Gordon Jacob of the military-band Folk Song Suite of 1923
fields.note: The Archive description says this appears to be the only 78-rpm recording of the Jacob orchestration; the Discogs label credit names Jacob as arranger. The Burgess Hill programme note says Jacob made the transcription in 1924 but that it was not published until 1942, so how Barlow’s 1939 orchestra obtained the score is not established here.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Vaughan Williams’s copyright in the music runs to the end of 2028 in the UK and EU; Jacob’s arrangement has its own term.
fields.note: The Vaughan Williams Foundation gives 2028 as the year copyright in his music expires. IMSLP marks the suite as not in the public domain in the EU. Composition and arrangement rights are separate from the recording.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU phonogram public-domain basis: commercial issue in 1940, before 1963
fields.note: The project’s eu-published-before-1963 rule applies to the English Columbia issue of 1940 and the American set of March 1940: the former 50-year phonogram term had expired before the 2013 extension. This is not United States or worldwide clearance and not a Creative Commons licence.

composer.epithet: He wrote down an Essex folk song in 1903, edited the English Hymnal and carried a Tudor psalm tune into the concert hall.

Composer, folk-song collector, hymn-book editor, teacher and conductor; Leith Hill Musical Festival, 1905–53

quote.text: In the next world, I shan’t be doing music, with all the striving and disappointments. I shall be being it.
quote.source: Vaughan Williams to Sylvia Townsend Warner, about a fortnight before his death in August 1958, as she recorded it in a letter

composer.background:
On 9 February 1875 Arthur Vaughan Williams, vicar of All Saints, Down Ampney, died after a brief illness. His third child, Ralph, born in the vicarage on 12 October 1872, was two. His widow Margaret, a Wedgwood, took the children to her family’s house at Leith Hill Place in Surrey. Aunt Sophy gave the boy piano lessons, and at six he wrote a piece called The Robin’s Nest. He went to Charterhouse in 1887 and to the Royal College of Music in 1890, where Hubert Parry taught him composition; in 1892 he went up to Trinity College, Cambridge, to read history as well as music.

Adeline Fisher, a cellist and pianist whose first cousin was Virginia Woolf, became his wife on 9 October 1897 at All Saints, Hove, three days before his twenty-fifth birthday. After a brief spell of study with Max Bruch in Berlin he went back to his post as organist at St Barnabas, South Lambeth, which he had held since 1895, disliked, and gave up in 1899.
